                                  14   II.      LEGAL STANDARD
                                  15            The Federal Arbitration Act (“FAA”) governs the Arbitration Agreement between the

                                  16   Parties. Arbitration Agreement § 1. The FAA declares “that a written agreement to arbitrate ...

                                  17   ‘shall be valid, irrevocable, and enforceable, save upon such grounds as exist at law or in equity

                                  18   for the revocation of any contract,’” and thereby establishes a “liberal federal policy favoring

                                  19   arbitration.” Moses H. Cone Mem’l Hosp. v. Mercury Constr. Corp., 460 U.S. 1, 24 (1983)

                                  20   (quoting 9 U.S.C. § 2). When parties enter into an arbitration agreement, the FAA “leaves no

                                  21   place for the exercise of discretion by a district court, but instead mandates that district courts shall

                                  22   direct the parties to proceed to arbitration on issues as to which an arbitration agreement has been

                                  23   signed.” Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v. Byrd, 470 U.S. 213, 218 (1985). Any doubts regarding the

                                  24   scope of arbitrable issues should be resolved in favor of arbitration. Green Tree Fin. Corp. v.

                                  25   Bazzle, 539 U.S. 444, 452 (2003).

                                  26            In determining whether to compel a party to arbitrate, the court must determine: “(1)

                                  27   whether a valid agreement to arbitrate exists and, if it does, (2) whether the agreement

                                  14          A.        Whether WFG Waived Its Right to Arbitrate
                                  15          Like other contractual rights, arbitration agreements may be waived. Armstrong v.

                                  16   Michaels Stores, Inc., 59 F.4th 1011, 1015 (9th Cir. 2023). “[T]he burden for establishing waiver

                                  17   of an arbitration agreement is the same as the burden for establishing waiver in any other

                                  18   contractual context.” Id. To prevail on a waiver claim, “the party asserting waiver must

                                  19   demonstrate: (1) knowledge of an existing right to compel arbitration and (2) intentional acts

                                  20   inconsistent with that existing right.” Id. “There is no concrete test to determine whether a party

                                  21   has engaged in acts inconsistent with its right to arbitrate;” instead, courts “consider the totality of

                                  22   the parties’ actions.” Hill v. Xerox Bus. Servs., LLC, 59 F.4th 457, 471 (9th Cir. 2023) (citation

                                  23   omitted). The party opposing arbitration bears the burden of establishing waiver, but that burden

                                  24   is not “heavy.” Armstrong, 59 F.4th at 1014. The party opposing arbitration need not establish

                                  25   prejudice. Id.

                                  26          The parties agree that Ms. Olson satisfied the first prong, so the Court considers only

                                  27   whether Ms. Olson has established that WFG’s intentional acts were inconsistent with its right to

                                  20           B.      Whether a Valid Agreement to Arbitrate Exists
                                  21           When assessing whether an arbitration agreement is enforceable, “generally applicable

                                  22   contract defenses, such as fraud, duress, or unconscionability, may be applied ... without

                                  26   govern the formation of contracts” apply to this analysis. Pokorny v. Quixtar, Inc., 601 F.3d 987,

                                  27   994 (9th Cir. 2010); see also Reichert v. Rapid Invs., Inc., 56 F.4th 1220, 1227 (9th Cir. 2022)
